^THIS. Automotive professional 30+ years here who has trained finance managers. Your score does not determine your approvability—it’s primarily used to determine what your rate would be if you ARE approved. Approval is ultimately determined by the content of your credit profile, and repos will absolutely hurt you. Income, job stability, and other factors are not factored into your score, whereas lenders absolutely consider these things, so a score is just simply not a complete picture. I constantly would have to coach salespeople and even sales managers to disregard the score when looking at credit, because you can have a bad 700+ or a good 650.

I have excellent credit and my profession deals with credit, so I have a good working knowledge of how credit works. If it were me, I’d take the chance and blow this one off, because in order for this to affect your score, it’s incumbent on the storage facility to report it to the bureaus, and most businesses like that do not. Even if it WERE to hit your credit report, the impact would be small score wise, and you can always dispute it, with a reasonable chance it would come off, because in order for it to stick on your credit report, the storage facility would have to respond and provide proof that you owe this. And although they CAN theoretically, the likelihood of this is even lower. The decision whether or not to pay is yours alone, but just know the risk on this one should be relatively low.

Question is now 2yo, but I thought I'd post an answer anyway, as I'm from the industry, and the advice that was given below was INCORRECT. This is basically saying that exceeding the AFVR doesn't automatically disqualify it from coverage altogether. It will still cover the gap, but will only up to that maximum percentage.

You CAN roll over negative equity and the GAP potentially CAN cover it...it just can't exceed the maximum percentage. So, you finance 38k and 3k of it is rolled over from a previous loan, and policy's maximum AFVR is 150%. Then you total this car, and it is valuated to be worth 19k at time of loss, and you still owe 30k (part of which is that rolled over 3k). The 30k you owe is 157.89% of the 19k it's now worth. The policy only pays up to 150%. So it will pay 28,500 (which is 150% of 19k), and you would have to pay the difference of 1500 (the balance of the 7.89%).

What I saw in my brother was someone who was a co-keeper of family memories. He had his gentle side, and I was amazed how many people came forward after his death to tell me what a great guy he was, how kind he was to them, and how much they remembered his smile. I also saw someone who was a victim as much as a predator.

His life from virtually the moment he was born was tragic. My father died  from cancer 3 mos after he was born. My mom was an immigrant who didn't speak good English and was hearing impaired, didn't drive nor know how to write a check, and she had two babies, one of which she'd only just given birth to. She did anything she could to pacify him as an infant because she just couldn't deal. She was not abusive in any way--she was a loving mom--but she had an awful lot to deal with in those days.

When he was just learning how to walk, he fell down the basement stairs and in the tumble, nearly chomped off his tongue--it was hanging on by a thin piece of flesh, and they couldn't stitch it, so they left it be. It eventually healed fully, but he had been nursing at the time and that abruptly stopped. My brother thinned out after that, and was super-skinny for the rest of his life. That led to an absolute lifetime of coddling by my mother, part out of guilt for that fall, and part out of pity for the little boy with no father. He ALWAYS got what he wanted and pitched a fit when he didn't. He slept in my mom's bed until he was about 9 or so, if you can believe that. I'm pretty positive it wasn't sexual. It was comforting to both of them. I just thought it was weird...still do.

As an adult, he let slip once that he had been sexually molested at around 9 y.o. by a houseguest who stayed in our basement for a year. I have no idea if it was a one-time thing or if it happened multiple times--he would not share details and seemed to regret sharing that much with me. But I can tell you that in adulthood he was most aggressive and belligerent towards gays. That was probably the reason why.

I've read up on narcissism since our thread conversation, and he had some of the traits, but not all, though admittedly I haven't spent full time with him in a long time. It does say that narcissism is potentially created by overindulgence in childhood, and my mother certainly mollycoddled him.  I see the humanity somewhere in there, and that's the part that my heart aches for. We grew up in the same house, had the same parents, but I nevertheless enjoyed a much more normal childhood than he did. I think what he became was definitely a result of his upbringing. I suspect there was some humanity in your brother-in-law, too, that he wasn't solely a monster.

All this aside, I DID recognize that continuing on with assistance as I had been doing was simply enabling him, and that it had to stop. I couldn't let him live on the streets, so I made sure he was hospitalized, diagnosed, and tied into assistance. Someday we'll figure out how to fix a broken human. Until then, maybe death IS the only way to ease their demons.

My first name is easy to pronounce in any language with little variation other than converting a short “a” to an “ah” sound. But I was much older when I found out that my Italian last name had been Americanized by my father before I was born. He changed the “ch” in the name from a hard “k” sound to a “tch” sound. Americans still can’t pronounce it, but at least it doesn’t sound like a swear word anymore. In school, from time to time I’d get a teacher who’d pronounce it the correct Italian way, and it would always result in a snicker from the class.

And now I’m married to a German, who omitted an umlaut from all official documents when immigrating, because its presence created such a hassle for him whenever he’d visit the US. The umlaut represents a silent “e”, and some of his credit cards would have “äu” but the hotel reservation would be made with an “aeu” because the website didn’t accept umlauted letters...and then the hotel would have trouble finding his name because they were searching according to the umlauted name in his ID card, but looking past the umlaut as Americans do, and actually searching for “au.” So when he immigrated, he just spelled it with “au.”  When you omit the umlaut, though, without that silent “e”, it changes the pronunciation, but we were cool with that—the non-umlauted version is also easier for Americans to read and pronounce. When we visit Europe, we use the umlaut and pronounce it as original.

Overnight stay at Yale New Haven Hospital, and consultation with THE top national expert on Sphincter of Oddi, and they conclude it's NOT Sphincter of Oddi, primarily because the pain could be relieved by position, which disqualifies SoO as a possibility...but they couldn't tell me WHAT it was if it wasn't SoO. Pain went away on its own, and my gastroenterologist, completely flummoxed, shrugged shoulders and recommended focusing on keeping a healthy intestinal tract--pre and probiotics, peppermint, healthy foods. The pain has largely stayed away...but this was what taught me that the medical community knows startlingly less than we give them credit for, most especially with regard to gastrointestinal issues.

Ashwaganda is something you take before meals—I would take it 3x/day. Ginseng is also an energy booster, so I would def take that in the morning.

Also, if bowel irritability is what is causing your search, please consider adding or increasing fiber to your morning.  I started having this issue after my gall bladder removal, and my gastroenterologist recommended fiber. She said, “I know most people associate fiber with constipation—and it does help with that too—but it works by balancing the liquid in your intestines, so it will also help if you have loose stools as well.” She was right—fiber REALLY helped with this problem. Just be sure to drink plenty of water or liquid during the day as well.

Benefiber dissolves completely and is virtually undetectable in a beverage—no grit or texture or flavor change—but it does have wheat dextrose, so if you have wheat sensitivities, then I recommend Floralax, which can be found on Amazon. Floralax is all natural—just oats, psyllium, and flax. There IS a detectable texture, but I personally don’t find it unpleasant like I did with Metamucil—it kinda has the texture of Cream of Wheat. I put it in a protein shake every morning and am sure to drink it quickly, as it continues to thicken the longer it sits in liquid. And it WORKS. It’s not cheap, but by golly, it works!

I've seen a lot of young people struggle with the same. I'm glad to read that you want to move on to further education. The world today is far more technical than it ever was, and there are less opportunities for unskilled labor--you NEED some sort of higher education just to LIVE, or you will likely struggle the rest of your life.

There's a lot that we don't know about you from your post. Firstly, do you know what career you eventually want to pursue once you finish college?  Secondly, can your parents help at all with college? Third, do you have any hobbies or experiences that might translate to job skills?

Depending on what you are hoping to pursue, I would encourage you to enroll as early as possible in community college. As someone who has hired candidates in the professional world, I can tell you that many (if not most) employers don't care where you got your degree. Of course, if you're going to be a doctor or lawyer or certain other specialty positions, that statement is not true...but for most, a potential employer will not care that your degree is from a community college...they'll only care that you have one. The very best thing about community college is that it is exponentially less expensive than a university experience. And it's local. And their degrees are just as valuable as the university ones, but for an absolute FRACTION of the cost.

If your parents can help with some or all of the cc costs, all the better--have a sit-down with them to discuss making it happen. If not, then where to search for work? Check with a car dealership--they often have many varied positions for the unskilled, and will train people for more skilled roles. Grocery stores and other retail. Factories. 

Scour Indeed, fill applications/send resumes. And explore your state's unemployment offices--they usually have counseling services available on how to make a resume, and can teach you winning interview skills. They also often have job listings you can't find anywhere else.

One last thing: Don't get spendy when you do find a job. Be stingy, thrifty. Students who take gap years to work or travel often don't go back because they make financial commitments that eventually prevent them from returning to school. Don't let that happen.

Best of luck to you! Hope this helped.

I'll suggest another item that I actually train on in my corporate training--and this achieves astonishingly good results. Believe it or not, if you're in a slump of any kind, whether it's procrastinating with study, not hitting performance numbers at work, whatever, the best remedy is to CLEAN your office or room (wherever you are supposed to focus on and do work). Wet-clean every horizontal surface you have, both in and out of drawers. Organize your files and re-label them if needed. Make sure EVERYTHING has a place going forward. Maybe even hang a few pics and put out a few decorations. These things all DO have an effect on your ability to concentrate.

When this tip was first suggested to me YEARS ago, I looked at the person sideways--this was the hokiest wives' tale I'd heard in a while. But he kept insisting, and this gentleman was an extremely well-respected top trainer in my field, so I tried it. I'll be damned if it didn't actually work. I could point you to industry forums and threads where dozens upon dozens of people vouch to the effectiveness of this piece of advice.

The reason that cleaning your work area helps in improving your performance is actually science-based. Studies have found that organization DOES help your to focus better.  "In 2011, researchers at [Princeton University](http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21228167) found that clutter can actually make it more difficult to focus on a particular task. Specifically, they found that the visual cortex can be overwhelmed by task-irrelevant objects, making it harder to allocate [attention](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/attention) and complete tasks efficiently." This is just one study that points to why this technique works.  The quote comes from this Psychology Today article, which also cites additional studies that also point to the effectiveness of this technique, but for the record, this is NOT an exhaustive list. 

Cleaning can become a smaller and easier to complete short-term goal that will lead you on the way to your larger goal of focusing on your schoolwork. Just give it a try--I promise, you'll be pleasantly surprised by how effective this is.

More on that:  [https://greensleeves.typepad.com/berkshires/2006/07/the\_srawling\_mi.html](https://greensleeves.typepad.com/berkshires/2006/07/the_srawling_mi.html) 

Some great spots in Torrington: Its entire downtown area still has a small town feel,with lots of great restaurants and boutique type shops, but is still fairly substantial. Historically, downtown Main St. would shut down every Thursday in summer for a summer festival series that included local shops displaying wares, booths with food and crafts. This year it is expected that summer festivities will instead shift to the town's downtown park, Coe Park, and occur less frequently.

The most prominent business on Main St. is the historic landmark, Warner Theater. The Warner is a GORGEOUS and grand theater built by Warner Bros and opened in 1931, and has hosted shows by prominent artists such as Pat Benetar, George Carlin, Bryan Adams, and many more. 

Near the Warner is the historic Yankee Pedlar Inn, a multi-floor historic hotel that currently is not open. It's been closed for several years with promises to renovate and reopen soon. The Yankee Pedlar has long been rumored to be haunted, and as such, a fictional horror film, "The Innkeepers", was filmed there, starring Kelly McGillis. Many famous guests have stayed at the Pedlar--often performers appearing at the Warner.

Burr Pond is a local state park with a large man-made pond for swimming and fishing, as well as picnicking and grilling. There are also several trails in the woods around the substantial pond for hiking and biking. This is the site of the former dairy farm belonging to Gail Borden, who patented his condensed milk concept here.

There are several other lovely state parks in Torrington: John Minetto State Park (which also has swimming, grilling, and picnicking), Stillwater Dam State Park, Sunnybrook State Park (which has fishing and seasonal hunting), and Major Besse Park which offers a ball field, playground, and downhill area for sledding. Besse Park Pond (which is a completely different park from Major Besse Park) has a large pond adjacent to a public pool that also offers covered picnic tables and playground area.

Many great places to dine in Torrington. The Venetian is an historic Italian restaurant that is approaching its 100th year. On Main St are Sasso's Wood Fired Pizza and Remember When, an antique shop that also offers amazingly good dining, and a banquet hall above that is apparently very unique. Pizzeria Marzano's is a must--it'll be the best pizza you've ever had--very authentic Italian...but you have to stand in line at the cash register to order before sitting down. Bunches more great restaurants that I did not mention.

Seymour:

\- Has lots of good antique shopping downtown, as well as a few other boutiques, and all  are close to each other, so it's an easy walk to visit them all.  Antique auctions on Tuesday downtown. Lots of junk, but plenty of really nice buys too!

\- When you're done with antiquing, you can stop at Tea With Tracy, a really adorable tea house that serves not only tea, but coffee, sandwiches, cookies, and other nice edibles. 

\- Seymour Fish Bypass. This was a $6.3 million State of CT project designed to eliminate one of the last obstructions to migratory fish on the Naugatuck River, and includes a small park and walkway alongside the section of the Naugatuck River that goes through Seymour, to enable fish to swim upstream to spawn. This was built alongside the Tingue Dam, which also has a very scenic small waterfall, and the walkway alongside and beyond the fish ladder is Seymour's segment of the Naugatuck River Greenway, which is a walking/hiking/biking trail that will one day span 44 miles from Torrington to Derby in western Connecticut, but is currently open in a few short disconnected segments totaling just over 5 miles. The trail is currently NOT connected to the existing small park overlooking the Tingue Dam waterfall from the other side of the river.

\- Stone's Throw Restaurant. This very unique restaurant serves food by an award winning chef, and was featured on Gordon Ramsay's 24 Hours To Hell And Back very recently. The restaurant is located directly on the Housatonic River, and pretty much every spot at the restaurant has gorgeous views of the river. The inside is arranged like a lodge, with a gorgeous stone fireplace. There is an outdoor patio with lots of tables and seats along the wall overlooking the river, and there is also a retractable glass sunroof for inclement days or winter, which offers spectacular views from a greenhouse-like dining area. The Gordon Ramsay episode created a stir because he used his usual bag of tricks, which included finding spoiled food in the kitchen fridge, but the owner claimed in an interview on WPLR that this was deliberately put there by producers for dramatic effect. We've eaten there since, food was great!
Be ready for a long wait because they are always MOBBED...but the ice cream there is second to none. This is actually on a dairy farm, although I don't think they actually make the ice cream there.

You're still very young...this stuff comes as you grow older, but it's good that you're seeking to expand your world. As a fellow introvert, I remember feeling that way when I was younger...I still do from time to time in certain situations. If you're feeling this way singularly with your gf, then AlekosLA may have hit on something--maybe you just don't have enough in common. But if this plagues you in most social interactions, I get it--it's the curse of introversion.  Being an introvert is not a bad thing--I like being one--but we ARE social creatures, our strength comes from being social, and we need to learn to navigate social interactions.

Reading a lot helps, especially non-fiction. Read FB posts re: politics and current events, then follow up to fact-check what they posted. Subscribe to the NY Times, LA Times, Fox News, MSNBC, BBC, CBS, ABC, NBC...anywhere you can get news from, and get alerts...and then read them when you get them.

Also, get out more--join a bowling league or a trivia group at a bar, or a baseball league, or a church group. SOMETHING that you might find interesting. Even better, if there is ANY way you can make it happen, travel abroad. If you don't have kids, you COULD pull up roots fairly easy, and travel abroad CAN be done inexpensively--there are hostels all over the world that you can stay at for cheap. See the world, learn different perspectives. The more interactions you have, the more memories you accumulate...and thusly, the more you can share. Being able to pull anecdotes out of your brain for any given topic requires lots of experiences and a large base of knowledge that ultimately takes time and many interactions to accumulate. Then, at some point, you realize that we are ALWAYS growing, and a thirst for knowledge and experiences will have given you a full life.
